Knife [.1] with leaf shaped ogee blade and wooden handle expanding towards the butt and bound with iron. With hide sheath [.2] with square tip, bound at the top with iron. [El.B 02/07/2007]
Kpinga. Multi-bladed iron throwing knife with curved and pointed elements. Handle formed of braided plant fibre.
Sape. Double-edged knife with iron blade. Carved wooden handle terminating in a human face with burnt detailing. Oval opening in handle.

Sape. Double-edged knife with iron blade decorated with punched dot design. Carved wooden handle terminating in a human face with glass bead eyes (one detached and missing) and burnt detailing including scarification.
Sape. Double-edged knife with iron blade decorated with punched dot design. Carved wooden handle terminating in a human face with glass bead eyes and burnt detailing.

Wili sape. Knife. Iron, double-edged blade with wooden handle wrapped in brass wire. Leather sheath with tip and mouth wrapped in flat copper wire. Used for shaving and other small purposes. Often is a payment in ceremonial exchange or purchase. Wili sape.

Kundi. A small bow harp, with a curved, wooden neck and a resonator made from wood and covered with hide. The resonator is a waisted oval shape, with two points at side and one at each end, and two round holes in the top. There are five plant fibre strings that come out from the resonator and are each wrapped round a cane tuning peg that slots into a hole in the neck. The neck is slightly cracked and two of the strings have broken.
Iron knife with wooden handle bound in copper wire and twisted copper cords. Decorated with brass studs. Sheath of hide over a framework of cane with twisted leather strap.

Iron knife with two double-edged blades either side of a rectangular grip bound with copper wire. Both blades are decorated on both faces along the central ridge with incised ornamentation in zig-zags or nicks. Possibly for shaving.

Kundi. A wooden bow harp, with a curved neck that terminates in a detailed carving of a human head with a headdress and a necklace of blue glass beads and fibre. The resonator is pointed at both ends with a scalloped waist, with a slight ridge along the almost-flat top; however, the underside of the resonator has a triangular cross-section. The resonator and part of the neck is covered with hide, and there are two round holes in the hide on the upper side of the resonator. There are five strings, each made from two strands of giraffe tail hair twisted together, that are strung between the resonator and the five tuning pegs that slot though holes in the upper part of the neck. The fourth string is broken.

An iron knife with a broad sickle shaped blade and a wooden haft. The shoulders are at different heights with the cutting edge side being lower. At the base of the blade are two circular perforations. The narrow tang is fitted into a cylindrical wooden haft, partially bound in wire; it has a wider cylindrical terminal.

An iron knife with a broad roughly sickle shaped blade and a wooden haft. At the base of the blade is a circular perforation through which a strip of leather has been tied and connects to the handle. At the base of the cutting edge is a roughly cylindrical protrusion. The narrow tang is fitted into a cylindrical wooden haft bound in wire.

A small iron knife with a leather sheath. The blade is double edged with an hourglass shaped shoulder. With a cylindrical wooden handle that has a flaring triangular base and a circular top with brass tacks. Decorated with alternating bands of metal binding. The leather sheath is rectangular and decorated with copper alloy binding. The knife is stuck inside the sheath. A section is missing from the circular top of the handle.
Trumbash. A throwing knife with several limbs that are all pointed and double edged. With a woven string handle that has been plaited.

A small iron knife with a leather sheath. The blade is double edged and tapers to a rounded end. The iron handle is bound in leather with a flaring, triangular end. The sheath is roughly triangular with a tapering end, it is decorated with raised moulding and leather tassels at the base. At the top is a loop, possibly for securing the knife to another object.

An iron knife with a broad roughly sickle shaped blade and a wooden haft. At the base of the blade are two circular perforations and roughly cylindrical protrusion. The narrow tang is fitted into a cylindrical wooden haft, partially bound in copper alloy wire.

An iron knife with a broad sickle shaped blade and a wooden haft. There is a pronounced midrib that follows the curve of the blade.  The shoulders are at different heights with the cutting edge side being lower. At the base of the blade are two circular perforations. The narrow tang is fitted into a cylindrical wooden haft with a wider cylindrical terminal. There are some cracks in the wood.
Trumbash. A throwing knife with several limbs that are all pointed and double edged. With a leather bound handle secured with string.

instruments.title: harpa, kordofon, musikinstrument, harp, musical instrument, kondi
Flûte à embouchure terminale à double encoche

Slit drum carved from a single piece of wood, used for signalling. The drum section is a hollow half-cylinder with a long oblong slit across the top. The drum is two-toned, with the side on one half of the slit being about one tone higher than the other. It is supported on two legs, and has a handle in the form of a carved human head at each end. There is a vertical perforation through the neck of each handle; however, one of them is blocked. There are incised numerals on each side.

Sanza, with eight cane keys arranged with the longest in the middle and the shorter keys at the edges. The keys are held in place with cane stitching, and are braced against two wooden bars. They are on top of a hollow resonator, which is almost oval in shape, but has a small square projection at one of the narrower end where the tops of the keys overhang. The resonator has a flat upper side and a rounded bottom. The flat top is secured in place with small wooden pegs, plant fibre, and twine.

household.title: Basketry hat made from woven dried grass. The rim is decorated with a dark down strip with zig zag decoration. The top of the hat is square.
Ndu kuna. Gourd with bulbous body and swelling at base of neck. Lengths of bark fibre knotted around waist. Used for carrying beer and water.
Ndu kuna. Gourd container with circular opening where the stem originally was. Lengths of bark fibre tied around waist. Ndu kuna.
Ndu kuna. Gourd container with circular opening where the stem originally was. Lengths of bark fibre tied around waist.

Kokpo. A basket used for carrying a pot of oil, sometimes used in circumcision ceremonies. A coiled basket with a round mouth, cylindrical body of striped natural and black fibres, and a square base, with four strips of cane attached at each corner to form feet. The rim is reinforced with cane wrapped in black fibre. A conical lid made from thick coiled basketry is attached by fibre, and has a loop at the apex. A long handle of twisted fibre is attached to the rim.
Zagbeli. Comb made of palm ribs lashed together with jute fibre. The frame of the comb is made from palm leaf stem bound in a zig-zag pattern with jute fibre to form the handle.

Zagbeli. Bound comb made by lashing palm ribs together with palm leaf fibre. Two types of binding made of palm leaf fibre; one has probably failed (the twisted vertical fibres) and another was put in place (the flat kind of binding).

Kolung bo. Large oval-shaped wooden bowl with two side handles, rounded body, and flat base. Handles features incised crosshatched decoration; rim of bowl decorated with incised parallel lines. Small chips in rim; scratches present in wood. Used for food.

Wili kolungbo. Wooden bowl with two side handles, rounded body, and flat base. A small circular perforation is present in each handle; a piece of raffia is tied to both handles through the perforations. Slits present in wood. Used for food.
Ngu. A piece of curved wood with a length of raffia tied around it. Used in a game; the user throws it to the ground, and tries to catch it in a noose when it bounces back upward.
Kiyaga. A shallow, square twilled basketry tray of natural colour, for winnowing grain. The rim is reinforced with two strips of cane, and each corner is reinforced with strips of fibre.
Wilingwa ka kpe akoro. Wooden pot scraper with handle and flat paddle with square end. Used to scrape outside of pots. Accretions.
Inga ka kpe akoro. Gourd-scraper used in pot-making; roughly circular with one flattened edge.
Inga ka kpe akoro. Gourd-scraper used in pot-making. Circular and broken in two; but still used in broken state.

A flat, square plaited basket with an open rectangular mouth, of black and natural coloured fibres forming stripes and diamond patterns. Thick plaited handle of natural fibre attached to the mouth. One thin strand of fibre knotted at the mouth, possibly as closure.
gbina mbipo. Trap for catching pigeons. Consisting of a dark twisted fibre net suspended between two wooden sticks. Each stick has a pointed end with traces of soil, possibly caused from use.

Rat trap. The trap is of multi-directional plaited cane, cylindrical in shape, tapering slightly toward a bound cane handle. Inside the trap are two wooden sticks with thorns attached to the inner surface near the entrance.
Rat trap. The trap is of multi-directional plaited cane, cylindrical in shape, tapering slightly toward a partially bound cane handle.

Ngwa. Walking stick with scorched circular indents along the shaft and a right-angled handle. Extending from the handle is a carved head, featuring scorched detailing, with three vertical scarification marks under each eye.

Circular wooden stool with central, spheroid support decorated with deeply incised wedges and circular foot. Seat is decorated around the perimeter with incised lines in triangular sections and a triangular cut-out close to one edge. Slightly chipped on foot and seat.
Ivory bark beater with a crosshatched pattern of pyramids on one flattened end; the other end is broken and rough.
Rat trap. Cylindrical trap of multi-directional plaited cane, tapering slightly toward a bound plant fibre handle. Inside the trap are four wooden sticks with thorns attached to the inner surface.
Rat trap. Cylindrical stake-and-strand dark-brown cane trap, tapering into a cone-shape at the closed terminus, with a large circular-hoop opening. Evidence of historic damage.
Kpakpali. Basketry hat with square crown, decorated with black bands and a basketry brim with a cane cross on the crown.

A small stool carved from a single piece of wood, stained with a black pigment. The seat is ovular and curves up at the shorter edges. The stool has four legs, each with a little sideways foot, and a stepped handle with a round hole drilled in the end. There is a small crack in the seat.

Ngwa. Walking stick with bands of bevelled carved squares upon the shaft and a right-angled handle. Extending from the handle is a carved head, featuring scorched detailing, with three vertical scarification marks under each eye.

garment.title: Kpakpali. Straw hat of natural and dark brown plant fibres, narrow brim with deep(it) crown, pair of stiffeners at crown fixed into a X position.
Ngaka or agba. Skirt made from long strips of banana leaves plaited over a broad waistband.
Ngaka or agba. Grass skirt consisting of long, flat strands of grass knotted over a broad waistband.
Grass circumcision skirt. Alternating groups of light and dark lengths of grass tied to a cord waistband. Used by boys for dancing. Tied in a roll.
Grass circumcision skirt. Alternating groups of light and dark lengths of grass tied to a cord waistband. Used by boys for dancing.
Grass circumcision skirt. Alternating groups of light and dark lengths of grass tied to a cord waistband. Used by boys for dancing. Rolled.
Woven hat with square top. Panel of dark brown decoration around the rim with geometric design in natural grass colour. Holes in each of the corners. Rim unravelling.
Woven hat with square top. Panel of dark brown decoration around the rim with geometric design in natural grass colour. Chevron pattern on upper surface in dark and natural colours. Body unravelling.

A view of a Zande homestead with a posed group of five women in the foreground showing a variety of Zande domestic objects and activities. These include a trough mortar and pestle, stirring a pot, sorting a pile of eleusine, ?winnowing grain, and grinding flour. Behind the group is a man dressed in a tunic and large pantaloons, holding a very large spear, probably used for hunting elephants or other large animals. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

A full length portrait of a Zande woman in the entrance to a homestead, wearing coiled metal arm and ankle rings and leaf pubic covering on a string. Set to both sides of the entrance are two shields leaning against the fence, which is made from stalks etc. The shield to the left seems to have a throwing knife placed on top of it. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

A full length portrait of a Zande woman in front of a hut carrying a small child in a broad skin carrier on her hip. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

A piled arrangement on a table (probably in front of a fence) of Zande carved wooden bowls and stools, as well as a throwing knife placed in front. It is possible that Buchta collected a number of Zande objects on his brief expedition to this part of Sudan. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

A woman preparing to immerse a basket of malted eleusine grain which is wrapped in banana leaves in a pool, an initial stage in the brewing of a beer type known as gbangara, a reddish-coloured eleusine brew.

A man (possibly Kisanga) immersing a basket of malted eleusine grain which is wrapped in banana leaves, an initial stage in the brewing of a beer type known as gbangara, a reddish-coloured eleusine brew. It is then spread out in the sun to germinate.

A woman immersing a basket of malted eleusine grain which is wrapped in banana leaves, an initial stage in the brewing of a beer type known as gbangara, a reddish-coloured eleusine brew. It is then spread out in the sun to germinate.
A portrait of two women wearing barkcloth aprons (agbaya), made from the bark of a species of fig-tree (Ficus platyphylla).

Two widows (dekurugbo) in the foreground (with shaven heads, one with string around torso) being ritually anointed with oil at the termination of their mourning period, when a feast is held. After a husband's death widows would have been expected to marry either his brother or another close male relative (levirate).
A woman wearing a striped woven cloth (ramu) and a small boy carrying a stick, with other dancers in the background, with one possibly seated on a wooden gong (gugu).

A widow (dekurugbo) in the foreground being ritually anointed on the hand with termite oil by a woman wearing a sash of white beads, at the termination of the mourning period when a feast is held. After a husband's death widows would have been expected to marry either his brother or another close male relative (levirate).
A group of men and boys at a dance. The men are wearing barkcloth loincloths (bagadi), straw hats and are carrying sticks.

A collection of stones outside a deceased persons hut, in preparation for the raising of a grave mound over the burial site (mura) close by. The hut is dilapidated since the pumbó or mortuary feast at which the mound is raised is often a year or more after burial. In front of the doorway is a tuka or spirit-shrine where medicines (ngua) are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead.
Portrait of a boy (identified as wiri Zaba, i.e. a son of Zaba) wearing a white cotton waist cloth.

A group of abinza (witchdoctors) dancing at a gathering held in Evans-Pritchard's own compound on the occasion of the ritual burial initiation of a new member (Evans-Pritchard's servant Kamanga) which facilitated the gathering of data on the abinza corporation. Kamanga's feet can be seen emerging from the hole.

A tuka or spirit shrine in a garden, showing a split stick, the ends bound at the top and a ritual offering in the split of the stick and on the ground below. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral spirit (atoro) favour for the garden.
A portrait of a man (identified as Kisanga).

A man at the home of Bambatu seated on a stool wearing a straw hat and barkcloth loincloth, tending an earthenware cooking pot on a small fire containing Bingiya (Bingia) medicine. This medicine was one of the most important of hunting medicines, although it was believed to have other effects also. Bambatu is the man to the right.
Women emptying dampened malted eleusine to germinate on the ground, covering them with further banana leaves to protect them from the sun, ready for the next stage of beer (gbangara) preparation.

A gathering of abinza (witchdoctors) held in Evans-Pritchard's own compound on the occasion of the initiation of a new member, Evans-Pritchard's servant Kamanga, which facilitated the gathering of data on the abinza corporation. They are dancing around a hole being dug for the ritual 'burial' of the initiate.
A portrait of a girl with braided hair (identified as a daughter of Prince Ngindö) wearing a bracelet, necklet and waist string, with her arm on her hip.
A man (identified as Windis or Zori, a subject of Gami, a commoner Governor) sitting on the ground within a homestead, his foot resting on the tail of an iwa (rubbing-board) oracle.
A standing group of four boys of varying ages, one wearing shorts, two others small loincloths (bagadi)
A standing group of four boys of varying ages, one wearing shorts, two others small loincloths (bagadi)
The back of a man's head (identified as Kamanga's), with his hand shading his eyes.

A binza (identified as Kamanga) standing in a homestead in full dancing apparel, including headdress. Kamanga was initiated in the abinza corporation at the instigation of Evans-Pritchard in order to gain ethnographic information about the corporation's medicines and ritual practices.

A binza (identified as Kamanga) standing in a homestead in full dancing apparel, including headdress. Kamanga was initiated in the abinza corporation at the instigation of Evans-Pritchard in order to gain ethnographic information about the corporation's medicines and ritual practices.
A portrait of a youth wearing a barkcloth loincloth (bagadi) and leaning on a stick.

A portrait of a youth (identified as Zakiri) in shirt and shorts, with a large old-style granary (type known as soro) in the background. A boy named Zakiri worked for Evans-Pritchard as a household servant during his fieldwork.
A portrait of a youth (identified as Khamsa) in shirt and shorts standing in front of a reed courtyard fence.

A man (identified as Bambatu) standing in a homestead wearing a white shirt and carrying a hat. To one side can be seen a tuka or spirit shrine with a gourd attached, probably containing medicines (ngua).

A man and two women spreading out banana leaves for dampened malted eleusine to germinate on. They will then be covered in further banana leaves to protect them from the sun, ready for the next stage of beer (gbangara) preparation.

A tuka or spirit shrine in the centre of a homestead, consisting of a split stick, the ends bound at the top, and next to it a taller tree trunk with a gourd (of medicines) hanging from it. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead. Beyond is a shelter with a roof supported on four columns, possibly with carved capitals, and a chair.

A woman immersing baskets (type known as bangiribambamba - eye-shaped weave) of malted eleusine grain which is wrapped in banana leaves, an initial stage in the brewing of a beer type known as gbangara, a reddish-coloured eleusine brew. It is then spread out in the sun to germinate.

A tuka or spirit shrine, consisting of a forked tree trunk or branch, with a bowl containing offerings set in the fork. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead. This shrine has numerous medicines growing around it, including sarawa, ranga ambiri and giango (cactus plant).

Women immersing baskets of malted eleusine grain partially wrapped in banana leaves, an initial stage in the brewing of a beer type known as gbangara, a reddish-coloured eleusine brew. It is then spread out in the sun to germinate.

A tuka or spirit shrine, consisting of a forked tree trunk or branch, with a bowl containing offerings set in the fork. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead. This shrine has numerous medicines growing around it, including sarawa, ranga ambiri and giango (cactus plant).

Women with large open-weave baskets (type known as bangiribambamba - eye-shaped weave) that are to be filled with beaten eleusine. This crop was once the most important base for porridge and beer, but has been displaced to some extent by manioc, a highly drought and pest resistent tuber, which is however somewhat less nutrious than flour produced from grain such as eleusine.

A portrait of a man (identified as Tupoi) with brimmed straw hat (kisikindi), with two other men either side of him, and in the foreground some large wooden vessels. Beyond is a large meeting shelter (possibly type known as baruti). This may indicate that the image was taken at Gangura's court.
A man (identified as Bambatu) standing on a road wearing a white shirt and hat.

A binza (identified as Kamanga) standing in a homestead in full dancing apparel, including headdress. Kamanga was initiated in the abinza corporation at the instigation of Evans-Pritchard in order to gain ethnographic information about the corporation's medicines and ritual practices.
A group of three men, two wearing barkcloth and one in shirt and waistcoat (half shaved head).  One of the men is identified as wiri Ondosi, i.e. a son of Ondosi.

A man (identified as Kamanga, one of Evans-Pritchard's servants) posed blowing a magic whistle (kura). Such whistles are mostly worn about the body and are used for a variety of purposes, such as to ward off witchcraft. They are made from plants and horns with magical associations, such as zerengbondo, a type of creeper.
A blind man or iravurari (unidentified) seated on the ground holding a long stick.

Two boys, one showing a slightly expanded abdomen (associated with malnutrition) and abdominal hernia, standing outside a hut with long eaves almost reaching the ground and a tunnel-like entrance way (probably a sleeping-hut for older children, possibly type known as barumai or dondomo).

Widows (dekurugbo) in the foreground being ritually anointed with oil by a specially designated woman at the termination of her mourning period, when a feast is held. After a husband's death widows would have been expected to marry either his brother or another close male relative (levirate).

A woman with heavy cicatrisation on her chest making "eyes" as a joke during the ritual anointment of widows at the termination of their mourning period, when a feast is held. Since she is wearing a man's brimmed straw hat (kisikindi), she may well be comically acting out the new attentions of men towards the widows who are free to remarry.

Two widows (dekurugbo) in the foreground (with shaven heads, one with string around torso) being ritually anointed with oil at the termination of their mourning period, when a feast is held. After a husband's death widows would have been expected to marry either his brother or another close male relative (levirate).

Major P. M. Larken, the District Commissioner for Yambio District (1911-1932), sitting on the ground with his arm around a girl, with a boy next to them. In front of them is a carved stool, and in the background a sleeping hut (type known as gbuguru).
Portrait of a man (identified as Kpakiti, a son of Prince Bavongara, son of King Gbudwe) wearing a decorated straw hat and seated in a cane chair, arm outstretched.

Male warrior (identified as Kuagbiaru) demonstrating the use of a wickerwork shield (kube), coming towards the camera with a raised spear. Although the use of shields was illegal under British adminstration, Evans-Pritchard had several examples made for him by those who still knew the craft.

Women preparing to put bundles of eleusine coracana (millet) grain into large openwork baskets (type known as bangiribambamba, with eye-shaped open weave), ready for immersing in a nearby pool. Once dampened, the grain is laid out in the sun to germinate, an intial stage in the brewing of millet beer, gbangara.

A Zande version of the widespread African game often known as mancala (an arabic word meaning 'to transfer', i.e. move game pieces from one hole to another). The Zande version (known as abanga) was sometimes carved, but is here set in the earth under the eaves of a hut or granary, with an old-style stool for a player visible beyond.

A small grass medicine shelter set within a garden. Since medicines to protect crops (such as bagbuduma) are vulnerable to damp and cold they were frequently placed in such shelters to protect them, or covered by an inverted pot or in the hollow of a tree.

A tuka or spirit shrine in the centre of a homestead with medicines growing at its base and two spears leant against it. A man (identified as Kisanga) is staining a carved stool (zagbali, mbata) in the background by applying a liquid to it from a clay pot boiling on a fire.
A man standing beside his coil-technique earthenware pots (pere). To one side is a bench seat (kitikpara) used by the maker.

Two men building up the clay inner wall of the common hut type known as gbuguru or gbasendeyo, which has long overhanging eaves creating a shaded area. This image shows how the walls are made, with relatively thin strips built up in layers by hand.
A full face portrait of a boy (identified as Nganzi).

A portrait of a woman (identified as na Namarusu, i.e. the mother of Namarusu) standing at the entrance to her hut. The eaves above the door are propped up with a pole, supporting some baskets stored above the eaves.

A group of abinza (witchdoctors) dancing around an initiate (Kamanga, Evans-Pritchard's servant and informant) at a ritual 'burial' ceremony. Kamanga's feet can be seen emerging from the hole. A mutilated onlooker (identified as Bitarangba) can be seen to the left.

Ahoro nzeme. Almost spherical bowl for oil with rolled rim; decorated with curving bands of semicircular indentations. On a tall stand with spherical area above the foot decorated with four large circular openings. Flared foot.

Kumbu buda. Globular pot with neck divided in two and rejoined at the mouth; everted rim. Each neck is decorated with a moulded human face. The upper part of the body is decorated with curving lines of tiny semicircular impressions. The area below the mouth is decorated all over with semicircular impressions. Possibly used to contain oil.
Akoro pësyë. Pot for vegetables. Flat base and flaring sides, circular mouth with rolled rim. Decorated around the body with bands of diagonal and crossing lines of impressed dots.

Akoro bakinde. Large pot of quartz-tempered red fabric for porridge. Small, slightly concave foot with flaring, rounded sides and everted rim. Decorated around the body with two bands of diagonal lines of impressed dots and one band of large impressed dots.
Sende ka me akoro. Specimen of pot-earth. Stored in a sealed tobacco tin.

sculpture.title: Carved wooden figure of a woman. These figures have no ceremonial significance. Today they are made for trade purposes. It is possible that similar figures once played a role in rituals of "secret societies".
Carved wooden female figure. For note see note on 27.2230.

Carved wooden male figure. Figure features a rounded hairstyle, vertical scarification marks on the cheeks, hands curved inward, and darkened shoulders, posterior area, and feet. Small white beads are attached as eyes; figure tilts slightly to one side. Cracks present in wood; historic pest activity.

Carved wooden male figure. Figure features a rounded hairstyle, vertical scarification marks on the cheeks, one arm curved downward, and one arm curved upward. Small white beads are attached as eyes; the genital area has been darkened; figure tilts slightly to one side.

Mbaiya. A side-blown horn, carved from an ivory elephant tusk. Near one end is a lozenge-shaped mouthpiece with a central hole. The tip has been carved with a hole that can be covered to vary pitch. Brown string is tied around the horn to form a loop.

textile.title: Ira or sleeping mat. Rectangular woven mat made from reeds; twill plaiting with a double border and the ends bent over to form a fringe.

Ire ga agangassi or mat used in boys' circumcision ceremonies. Rectangular mat woven from two colours of reed; design of two rows of concentric diamonds; twill plaiting with a double border and the ends bent over to form a fringe; red powdery pigment on one side of the mat, possibly ochre.

Iwa. Rubbing board oracle, used for divination. Consists of two wooden pieces tied together with a thin fibre rope. One piece of wood is circular with a cylindrical top protrusion; the other is circular with two legs and a roughly oval side protrusion. Used by rubbing the upper piece against the lower piece after a question is asked of the oracle; an answer is dependent on whether the upper piece sticks or slides off the lower piece.

A rectangular piece of barkcloth with visible beater marks and areas of red pigment, made from three panels of barkcloth sewn together using thick light coloured fibre. Sewn patches and repairs, also using thick light coloured fibre.
A square piece of barkcloth, dyed black, made from two panels stitched together. There are visible beater marks, and eight sewn patches of barkcloth attached using dark coloured fibre.

Roko. Rectangular length of undyed barkcloth made from four horizontal panels. There are visible beater marks as well as sewn patches with light-coloured plant fibre. There is evidence of historic damage.
A rectangular piece of light brown barkcloth, with distinctive small square beater marks.
A rectangular piece of barkcloth dyed red, with distinctive small square beater marks.
